```{r setup, include = FALSE}
has_data <- requireNamespace("StMoMo", quietly = TRUE) && requireNamespace("demography", quietly = TRUE)
has_gg <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, eval = has_data, message = FALSE)
```

This vignette forecasts mortality for France with Human Mortality Database
(HMD) data (`demography::fr.mort`), compares models in an honest rolling-origin
backtest, and combines them in an ensemble. A second example with England &
Wales (`StMoMo::EWMaleData`) shows a case where the classic Lee-Carter
intervals are too narrow.

```{r}
library(mortensor)
library(data.table)
```

## Data

Women and men aged 30 and over, 1950-2006, with single years of age up to 99
and an open interval 100+ (aggregated from the HMD's 110+ table):

```{r}
fr <- suppressWarnings(as_mt_data(demography::fr.mort, years = 1950:2006))
fr <- mt_regroup(fr, age = 30:100)
fr
```

```{r, eval = has_data && has_gg}
mt_plot_rates(fr)
```

## Models

All models share one interface. Each returns simulated paths of future
death rates.

| Constructor | Model |
|---|---|
| `rwd()` | Random walk with drift on log rates per age (benchmark) |
| `lee_carter()` | Lee-Carter, Poisson (Brouhns et al. 2002) or SVD (Lee and Carter 1992) |
| `tucker3()` | Tucker3 tensor decomposition of the age x period x stratum array, fitted jointly for women and men |
| `arima_series()`, `ets_series()` | ARIMA and exponential smoothing per age (package forecast) |
| `apc_bayes()` | Bayesian age-period-cohort model (package bamp; see its vignette) |
| `ensemble()` | Mixture of the draws of several models |

```{r}
fit_lc <- mt_fit(lee_carter(), fr)
head(mt_parameters(fit_lc)[parameter == "b"])
fit_t3 <- mt_fit(tucker3(), fr)
fit_t3$fits$fit_pct
```

## Backtest

`mt_backtest()` refits the model on data up to each origin and scores
predictive draws of the observed log death rates in the following ten years.
Scores are averaged over ages, years ahead, sexes and origins. Smaller CRPS
and WIS are better; well-calibrated 50%, 80% and 95% intervals contain about
50%, 80% and 95% of the observations.

```{r}
origins <- c(1986, 1989, 1992, 1995)
specs <- list(rwd(), lee_carter(), lee_carter(jump_off = "observed"), tucker3())
bt <- rbindlist(lapply(specs, function(sp) {
  b <- mt_backtest(sp, fr, origins = origins, h = 10, n_draws = 200)
  if (isTRUE(sp$params$jump_off == "observed")) b[, model := "Lee-Carter (observed jump-off)"]
  b
}))
mt_score(bt, by = "model")[order(crps)]
```

```{r, eval = has_data && has_gg}
mt_plot_coverage(bt)
```

Scores by horizon show how quickly accuracy deteriorates:

```{r}
dcast(mt_score(bt, by = c("model", "horizon")), horizon ~ model, value.var = "crps")
```

## Ensemble

An ensemble mixes the paths of its components. With `weights = "crps"` the
weights come from an inner backtest on the last years of the training data,
so they never use the years being forecast.

```{r}
ens <- ensemble(lc = lee_carter(jump_off = "observed"), t3 = tucker3(), rw = rwd(), weights = "crps")
bt_ens <- mt_backtest(ens, fr, origins = origins, h = 10, n_draws = 200)
mt_score(rbind(bt, bt_ens), by = "model")[order(crps)]
```

## Forecast to 2030

```{r}
fit_ens <- mt_fit(ens, fr)
fit_ens$weights
fc <- mt_forecast(fit_ens, to = 2030, n_draws = 1000, seed = 2026)
fc
```

```{r, eval = has_data && has_gg}
mt_plot_forecast(fc, ages = c("40", "65", "80", "95"))
mt_plot_age(fc, periods = c(2007, 2030))
```

Life expectancy at 65, computed path by path:

```{r}
e65 <- life_expectancy(fc, at = 65)
e65[period %in% c(2007, 2020, 2030), .(label, period, q0.025, q0.5, q0.975)]
```

```{r, eval = has_data && has_gg}
mt_plot_life_expectancy(fc, at = 65)
```

## A cautionary example: England & Wales

For men in England & Wales, Lee-Carter fitted to 1961 onwards forecasts the
decade after each origin with intervals that are far too narrow, and is less
accurate than the random walk. Lee-Carter intervals reflect only the
uncertainty of the period index; when the age pattern of mortality
improvement changes, as it did for British men from the 1970s, the
constant `b_x` misses it.

```{r}
ew <- as_mt_data(StMoMo::EWMaleData)
ew <- mt_regroup(mt_set_grid(ew, age = single_ages(30, 100, open = FALSE)), age = single_ages(30, 100, open = FALSE))
bt_ew <- rbind(
  mt_backtest(lee_carter(), ew, origins = 1996:2001, h = 10, n_draws = 200),
  mt_backtest(rwd(), ew, origins = 1996:2001, h = 10, n_draws = 200),
  mt_backtest(tucker3(), ew, origins = 1996:2001, h = 10, n_draws = 200))
mt_score(bt_ew, by = "model")
```

Backtests like this one are the reason mortensor reports interval coverage
alongside accuracy: a model can rank well on point accuracy and still give
misleading uncertainty.

## References

Brouhns N, Denuit M, Vermunt JK (2002). A Poisson log-bilinear regression
approach to the construction of projected lifetables. *Insurance: Mathematics
and Economics* 31(3): 373-393.

Lee RD, Carter LR (1992). Modeling and forecasting U.S. mortality. *Journal of
the American Statistical Association* 87(419): 659-671.

Bracher J, Ray EL, Gneiting T, Reich NG (2021). Evaluating epidemic forecasts
in an interval format. *PLoS Computational Biology* 17(2): e1008618.
